question: What is the biggest risk of reusing disposable syringes in a clinic?

options.B: Severe allergic reactions to leftover air
options.C: Permanent numbing of the injection site
options.D: Immediate breakdown of the plastic barrel

explanation: You've got this! Reusing syringes transfers tiny traces of blood and germs from person to person, spreading serious viruses like HIV and hepatitis. Always use a fresh syringe!

question: Why do many people in local communities prefer getting injections from informal medicine shops?

options.A: Oral medications are completely unavailable in cities
options.B: Government policy requires informal shops to give shots
options.C: They believe injections work much faster than pills
options.D: Injections are always cheaper than tablets

explanation: It's a common belief that shooting medicine straight into the body heals you faster than swallowing a pill. As nurses, patient education on safe administration is key here!

question: What does 'parenteral route' mean when talking about how diseases spread?

options.A: Entry through a break in the skin via needles or sharps
options.B: Inhalation of airborne droplets through the nose
options.C: Ingestion of contaminated food or drinking water
options.D: Spread through direct skin-to-skin physical contact

explanation: Think of parenteral as bypassing the skin barrier completely—usually when a contaminated needle or sharp punctures the tissue directly. Simple and clear!

question: Why can a needle look perfectly clean yet still carry a dangerous virus?

options.A: Microscopic traces of infected blood remain inside the hollow bore
options.B: Skin bacteria react with the metal to create new pathogens
options.C: The virus travels through the air surrounding the needle
options.D: Plastic needles absorb viruses and release them later

explanation: Even if you can't see it, an invisible film of fluid inside a needle hub holds enough viral particles to cause a new infection. That's why we never reuse needles!

question: Which organ in the body is the main target for both Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C?
explanation: Spot on! Both hepatitis B and C viruses attack liver cells, causing inflammation and long-term damage if left untreated.

question: A patient is shocked to test positive for Hepatitis C years after getting an unsterile injection. Why did it take so long to show up?

options.A: The virus often hides in the body silently for a long time before causing symptoms
options.B: The virus only becomes active when a person eats contaminated food
options.C: Hepatitis C instantly destroys the immune system within twenty-four hours
options.D: Antibodies against the virus disappear completely after a few months

explanation: Hepatitis C is known as a silent virus. It can quietly damage the liver over many years without making the person feel sick right away.

question: What is septicemia?

options.A: Presence of multiplying bacteria in the bloodstream
options.B: Inflammation limited to the outer layer of skin
options.C: A localized collection of pus in a single muscle
options.D: Sudden paralysis caused by a damaged nerve

explanation: Septicemia happens when bacteria get past local defenses and start multiplying in the general blood circulation, making the patient very ill all over.

question: A patient comes back three days after an injection with a hot, swollen, throbbing lump at the site. What is this most likely?
explanation: That classic combo of throbbing pain, heat, swelling, and a lump usually points to a bacterial abscess from an unsterile injection that may need draining.

question: Which nerve is most at risk when a gluteal (buttock) injection is given with poor technique?
explanation: Great nursing knowledge! The sciatic nerve runs deep in the lower buttock, so injections must be placed carefully in the upper outer quadrant to avoid it.

question: Why should nurses rotate injection sites for patients who need frequent medications?

options.A: It ensures the medication reaches the bloodstream much faster
options.B: It stops bacteria from multiplying on the surface of the skin
options.C: It gives previous tissue time to heal instead of forming hard scar tissue
options.D: It prevents the needle from becoming dull during the procedure

explanation: Sticking the exact same spot over and over causes fibrous scar knots, which hurt the patient and make drug absorption difficult. Rotating sites keeps tissue healthy!

question: Why is it important to ask patients if they have visited patent medicine vendors when taking their history?

options.A: Hospital records automatically track all purchases made in private shops
options.B: Many informal vendors administer unsterile injections that patients forget to mention
options.C: Patent medicine vendors are legally required to report side effects
options.D: Patients only get infections when visiting registered general hospitals

explanation: Patients often think of informal drug purchases as casual and might forget to mention them. Asking directly helps us catch hidden risks like unsterile shots!

question: A patient has a red, swollen, tender gluteal injection site. What extra sign would tell you the sciatic nerve might be involved?

options.A: Bleeding from the puncture hole on the skin surface
options.B: Numbness, tingling, or weakness radiating down the leg
options.C: High fever and generalized body shivering
options.D: Yellowish discoloration of the eyes and skin

explanation: When a nerve is irritated or hit, it sends warning signs down its pathway—like pins and needles, burning pain, or weakness in the leg.

question: What is the main goal of giving post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) right after an accidental needle stick?

options.A: To cure a chronic bacterial skin infection
options.B: To prevent the establishment of a viral infection
options.C: To numb the skin and prevent local tissue scarring
options.D: To relieve muscle spasms around the injury site

explanation: PEP uses quick antiviral meds to stop a virus from taking hold and multiplying after an accidental exposure. Every minute counts!

question: How is a painful muscle abscess caused by an unsterile injection usually managed?

options.A: Apply tight bandages to squeeze the trapped fluid out through the skin
options.B: Massage the lump firmly to help disperse the pus into surrounding tissue
options.C: Assist with surgical incision and drainage while maintaining sterile dressings
options.D: Advise the patient to ignore the lump until it dissolves on its own

explanation: Trapped pus has to come out! An abscess requires sterile incision and drainage, followed by proper wound care and antibiotics to help the patient heal.

question: Why is it a bad safety practice for healthcare workers to recap used needles?

options.A: It is the leading cause of accidental needlestick injuries
options.B: It makes the needle too dull for future use
options.C: It contaminates the plastic barrel with air bubbles
options.D: It violates hospital rules regarding medication labeling

explanation: Trying to guide a used needle back into its tiny cap is the easiest way to slip and prick your own finger. Safety first—never recap!

question: Where should a used injection needle go immediately after you give an injection?

options.A: Inside your pocket until you reach the utility room
options.B: Directly into a puncture-resistant safety box
options.C: Back into the original plastic wrapper on the desk
options.D: On top of the medication tray for later sorting

explanation: Always drop sharps straight into a designated safety box kept right beside you. Never carry them around or leave them on trays!
